A close reading for the week

“O, she’s warm!”

The Winter’s Tale · Act 5, Scene 3

Sixteen years after his jealousy seemed to kill his wife, a king is shown her statue. It moves. The scene may be Shakespeare’s most audacious ending, and it asks the audience to do what the king is asked to do: awake their faith.

PaulinaIt is requir’d
You do awake your faith.1 Then all stand still;
Or those that think it is unlawful business
I am about, let them depart.

LeontesProceed:
No foot shall stir.

PaulinaMusic, awake her: strike! Music.’Tis time; descend; be stone no more; approach;
Strike all that look upon with marvel.2 Come;

  1. 1

    The condition

    “It is requir’d / You do awake your faith.” Before the miracle comes a demand: those who cannot believe should leave. Paulina addresses Leontes, and through her Shakespeare addresses the audience. The statue scene breaks every rule the play has set up so far, since Hermione’s death was reported and mourned sixteen years ago, and Paulina asks us to accept it as an act of faith. Sceptics may depart. No one does.

  2. 2

    The spell

    Paulina’s command is a string of imperatives (descend, be stone no more, approach, strike with marvel) spoken over music. It sounds like conjuration, and she has just insisted her business is not “unlawful”. The scene walks a careful line: in 1611 a resurrection by magic risked the charge of witchcraft, so Paulina insists her spell is lawful while the stage performs a wonder. The ambiguity is deliberate and it is the source of the awe.
